# **Filler tokens on DeepSeek V4 Flash: testing a parallel-attempts hypothesis**

[https\://github.com/orvelte/fillertokensminiproject](https://github.com/orvelte/fillertokensminiproject)   
olivia velte

## **Question:** Filler tokens (e.g \[...\] between a question and its answer) improve accuracy without any visible reasoning ([blog post from Ryan Greenblatt](https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/recent-llms-can-use-filler-tokens), [Reading Between the Dots: Decoding Hidden Computation across Filler Tokens](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.03502), [Not All LLM Reasoning is Visible in the Chain-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22925)). Since filler tokens can only add width (more positions running the same layers) and not more serial depth, any benefit must come from doing more work side by side. Thus, current guesses at the mechanism of filler token benefits are that the model runs **several solution attempts in parallel** across the extra positions and aggregates them at the answer, functioning as an internal best-of-N.

These findings update the parallel-attempts hypothesis and suggest **two components to filler token’s benefits** (in DeepSeek V4 Flash): would need white box methods to separate them (see below)

1. **A small steadying effect (less interesting).** On questions the model already usually gets right, filler makes it right a bit more often (+8 points). A majority vote or a more confident model would produce the same effect, so black-box data can't attribute it.   
2. **A large, item-specific noise reduction**. On some questions, filler cuts out the arithmetic mistakes made while working out `y`, flipping them from almost always wrong to mostly right. This includes questions where the model almost never gave the right answer without filler.

## **What was done:**

* **Model and task:** DeepSeek V4 Flash via API in non-thinking mode, with zero reasoning tokens verified. Brauer et al.'s system-of-equations task: variables defined through a chain x → c₁x → y → c₂y → answer, plus distractor variables.  
* **Prompt:** 10-shot, with filler in the few-shot examples. The `Filler:` label is kept in the no-filler baseline, so the only difference between conditions is the filler tokens themselves.  
* **Uplift replicated:** with 100 dots, sampled accuracy rose from 46.5% to 62.1% (300 items × 16 samples at T=1).  
* **Main test:** per-item pass rates with and without filler. Items were classified by their no-filler answer distribution, using held-out sample halves to avoid regression to the mean. Temperature controls at T=0.7 and 0.4.  
* **Follow-ups:**   
  * Error-type decomposition  
  * Filler disruption at different locations with a matched-position control  
  * Analysis of Brauer's released white box (lens) decodes

## **Findings:**

**1\. The model isn't simply going with its most common answer (majority voting is falsified) and filler can fix questions the model usually gets wrong. Making the model more confident didn’t reproduce the effect.**

* If the model voted over internal attempts, items whose most common no-filler answer is incorrect should stay flat or get worse, because voting amplifies the most common answer. They instead improved by **23 pp \[17, 29\]**, and only 12.5% got worse.  
* This rules out the simplest concrete version of the parallel-attempts hypothesis. Baherwani et al. had speculated about multi-candidate exploration in filler but hadn’t tested anything concretely.  
* Lowering temperature to 0.7 or 0.4 moved those same items by only about 1–2 pp, with intervals spanning zero.  
* "Filler just makes the model more confident" would mimic voting. This control removes that confound and shows filler adds real computation beyond just sharpening.

**![][image1]**

**2\. Filler produces answers the model essentially never outputs without it.**

* Of 42 items with zero correct answers in 48 no-filler samples, 14 got at least one correct answer with filler, and 4 got a majority. This group improved in both runs (+18 pp and \+15 pp).  
* This rules out selection among the model's existing outputs. It does **not** rule out internal attempts, since internal computations needn't appear as sampled outputs.

![][image2]

**3\. Filler tokens help a lot on some questions and not at all on most.**

* 48 items jumped by 50 points or more, 3 fell that far, and 128 didn't move.  
* This rules out a uniform small boost. The effect is item-specific.

![][image3]

**4\. Positions behave as interchangeable (weak evidence).**

* Disrupting an 8-unit block of a 25-dot filler early, middle, or late (72–79%) costs about what simply having 8 fewer clean positions costs (78%).  
* This is evidence against a rigid, position-ordered chain, and fits Baherwani et al.'s finding that the useful signal is spread across the filler span. It sits in tension with Brauer's position-specific causal content on V3. **Caveat:** 33 items with intervals of ±10–12 points; an early-position effect of up to about 18 points can't be excluded.

![][image4]

**Component 2 from the updated hypothesis could be explained by 2 mechanisms, and likely needs white box methods to separate them definitely:**

1. **Mechanism 1 (H1): Parallel attempts with a better-than-vote selector** (a more specified form of the original hypothesis).  
   1. Several partial computations of `y` run at once, and the answer position combines them using something smarter than a vote, for example weighting attempts by internal confidence or consistency.  
* *To explain finding 1*, the selector must be able to favour a minority answer, so it needs some internal signal of which attempt is right. It's unclear what that signal would be for arithmetic.   
* *White box work would expect to see:* distinct candidate values of `y` held simultaneously (at different positions or superposed), and **independent manipulability** (changing the input to one attempt shifts that attempt's candidate without touching the others).  
2. **H2: One computation, spread across positions to reduce interference.**  
   1. There is only one computation of `y`, but its sub-parts (multiplication c₁x, the addition or subtraction, and the separate number features for magnitude and modular structure) run on different positions instead of competing for space in a single residual stream. The parallelism is *within* one computation, like the parallel pathways found in model addition circuits, instead of *across* attempts.  
* *Fits:* finding 5 (positions interchangeable, if sub-parts are placed flexibly), Brauer's Figure 4 (filler looks like the ordinary single-pass computation spread across positions)  
* *White box prediction:* positions hold different *components* of one value, not complete rival values. Removing positions should *degrade precision* (errors scattered near `y`), not switch between discrete alternative answers.

Tested uplift on other open weight models just to see if white box methods could be feasible, didn’t look too promising (this was as expected): 

![][image5]

**Limitations**

* One model, one task family, one main filler type (100 dots).  
* The Brauer reanalysis used a different model (V3) and task (2-fact addition), because system-of-equations decodes weren't released.
